newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE shrugs off Bosnian Moslem claim of poll abuse.
newsitem.headline: OSCE shrugs off Bosnian Moslem claim of poll abuse.

text.p: International organisers of Bosnia's elections on Sunday shrugged off Moslem claims of fraud on Serb territory, saying it was not up to either side to rule on the validity of the polls.

Agota Kuperman, spokeswoman for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said all sides had failed to deliver on promises to create conditions for free and fair elections, but had nevertheless agreed to take part.

Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic's SDA (Party of Democratic Action) announced at the close of Saturday's countrywide polling that it would not recognise the Serb results -- raising the prospect of gridlock over the creation of joint institutions based on the vote.
In what amounted to a public rebuke, Kuperman said all political parties had been able to conduct campaigns and all eligible citizens had had a chance to vote.
"It is not up to the SDA to determine whether the results of the election in either entity are legally valid. That certification is the sole responsibility of the OSCE," she told reporters.
Kuperman said the OSCE considered the polls were almost entirely free of abuse and added that preliminary reports from observers in the field suggested they were satisfied with what they saw.
"The SDA agreed to participate in these elections knowing full well that a state of perfection...had not been achieved," she said.

Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. architect of the Dayton peace agreement which ended Bosnia's war last November, said the elections had been largely trouble-free and dismissed the SDA complaint as "no big deal".
"We always knew there would be problems about the elections," he said in Sarajevo after returning from a meeting with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade.

Holbrooke was due to leave for Brussels later on Sunday to brief NATO countries on the elections and efforts to push ahead with the creation of common institutions designed to try and reunite the country after 3-1/2 years of war.
Analysts said the SDA manoeuvre was an opening shot in an expected post-election jostle for power.

The Dayton accord envisages a national collective three-man presidency with Serb, Moslem, and Croat representatives and a national House of Representatives from which a Council of Ministers will be drawn.
In what appeared to be their response, Bosnian Serb authorities on Sunday instructed their officials to stop counting votes in the Serb Republic.
OSCE organiser Nicole Szulc said the president of the republic's election commission had sent a letter to all counting stations calling off the count.
She said she had no other details, but a high-level OSCE team had left for the Bosnian Serb stronghold of Pale to try and resolve the issue.
"We are now going to see a lot of games played, it is almost as if they feel they have to do this," said one OSCE source.
